label: Contemporary
rationale: The best-documented working band on the West Coast, recorded where it worked. Over three nights in September 1959 Lester Koenig's Contemporary recorded Shelly Manne's quintet live at San Francisco's Black Hawk and issued the music as four LPs (S1, S5); Volume 1 is the set's opening statement — 'Summertime', 'Our Delight', 'Poinciana', 'Blue Daniel' at twelve and thirteen minutes apiece, a club band stretched out with nowhere to hide. Consensus across independent listing traditions is unusually strong for a live volume: the Penguin Guide gives it four stars and a Crown, the Rolling Stone Jazz Record Guide five stars (both via S1's ratings table, citing the Penguin Crown albums list), and AllMusic rates it four stars with Scott Yanow writing that 'the extended performances are easily recommended to straight-ahead jazz fans' (S1, S2). Lineage: it is the West Coast counterpart of the club documents this canon already holds — A Night at the Village Vanguard, A Night at Birdland, At the Cafe Bohemia, Sunday at the Village Vanguard — and Contemporary's house sound on this date is part of why those records are studied. Session gravity: Joe Gordon, the bop trumpeter who had come through Dizzy Gillespie's and Art Blakey's bands; Richie Kamuca, one of the warmest Lester Young-derived tenors on the coast; Victor Feldman, the London-born pianist and vibist; and Monty Budwig, Manne's bassist of the period (S1, S3, S4). Discovery value: the Manne who appears in this canon so far is a leader of a Broadway-song trio date (My Fair Lady); this is the hard-blowing club band, and the venue — the Black Hawk — is a place the canon's place map does not yet hold.

ballot.album: Shelly Manne & His Men — At the Black Hawk, Vol. 1 (1959)
ballot.case_for: The reported Penguin Guide Crown and four stars, Rolling Stone five stars, and AllMusic four stars provide substantial critical support, with Scott Yanow explicitly recommending the extended performances to straight-ahead listeners (S1–S2). Manne, Joe Gordon, Richie Kamuca, Victor Feldman, and Monty Budwig make this a compelling working-band document: the extended treatments of “Summertime,” “Our Delight,” and “Poinciana” foreground sustained ensemble interaction rather than studio polish (S1–S3). Its strongest discovery-canon claim is as a defining document of Manne’s live quintet and a vivid West Coast counterpart to the canon’s better-known New York club recordings.
ballot.case_against: The dossier establishes the Black Hawk engagement’s stature more securely than it establishes why Volume 1, specifically, is the indispensable standalone statement rather than one strong installment of a larger document. The Penguin and Rolling Stone judgments are supplied through a secondary ratings table, so their provenance merits verification; this limits evidentiary confidence without establishing that the underlying judgments are dependent (S1). Personnel connections and geographic importance strengthen the case, but the dossier supplies little demonstrated downstream influence or detailed criticism showing why these performances rise from excellent straight-ahead jazz to a load-bearing canonical album.
ballot.disagreement: Reference 1 rates the album contested, finding the album-specific consensus and Volume 1’s primacy insufficiently established; Reference 2 rates it consensus_core, treating the critical honors and defining live-band achievement as decisive. Both agree on strong priority and unambiguous scope. Reference 1 questions the independence of the reported ratings, but the supplied evidence does not establish that Rolling Stone’s judgment derives from Penguin.
ballot.recommendation: The council proposes that John give Volume 1 strong consideration as a defining Manne quintet document, while verifying the critical citations and its standing within the Black Hawk series.
